PullRequest.Title: Authenticate GitHub marketplace API requests via RFC 8693 token exchange
PullRequest.Body:
> **Scope: GitHub auth-enabled path only.** This is the follow-up PR deferred from microsoft/vscode#325804. It implements the **GitHub** side of the auth-enabled Private Marketplace called for in microsoft/vscode#325412 — RFC 8693 token exchange at the deployment's embedded Authorization Server, `onDidChangeSessions('github')` invalidation, and the GitHub test scenarios. The Entra/Microsoft path is unchanged here (it lives in #325804).

Stacked on microsoft/vscode#325804 (which is itself stacked on microsoft/vscode#325331). Because those are cross-fork PRs whose head branches live only in `mcumming/vscode`, GitHub won't let this PR base on the #325804 branch, so it bases on `main` and the commit range below currently **includes #325331's and #325804's commits**. It will reduce to just the two GitHub-auth commits once those merge.

Completes the GitHub auth-enabled portion of microsoft/vscode#325412 (the Entra path is covered by #325804).

## Summary

microsoft/vscode#325804 made the marketplace's API requests authenticate for the **Entra/Microsoft** provider by negotiating a resource-scoped bearer token via RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata (PRM) discovery. This PR does the same for the **GitHub** provider.

The difference is token acquisition. VS Code's Microsoft/MSAL provider mints a resource-scoped token directly (`getSessions(..., { authorizationServer })`, RFC 8707). VS Code's GitHub provider has no resource-token support, so when the marketplace index is `[Authorize]`-gated (RFC 9728 `401`) the client exchanges the user's **existing GitHub session token** at the marketplace's advertised Authorization Server using the **RFC 8693 token-exchange grant**. The AS returns a first-party `at+jwt` bound to the marketplace resource (`aud = resource`), which is then presented on the index retry and every protected API request.

The raw GitHub token is **only ever sent to the AS token endpoint**, never to the resource server; both the AS and its discovered token endpoint are validated with a same-origin-HTTPS guard (fail-closed) before the token is sent, and `followRedirects: 0` prevents a redirect from forwarding it elsewhere. Unlike the Entra scheme there is **no server-side eligibility verdict** on the GitHub path — access is decided entirely by the existing client-side `checkAccess()` gate; there is no `/eligibility` POST.

## Commits

Because #325804's head branch lives only in `mcumming/vscode`, GitHub cannot base this PR on it, so it targets `main` and the range shows #325804's commits (until it merges) followed by:

1. **Authenticate GitHub marketplace API requests via RFC 8693 token exchange** — `GitHubGalleryAccountProvider.getAccount(serviceIndexUrl)` now discovers the protected resource (RFC 9728), validates the RFC 8414 issuer, and exchanges the default account's GitHub session token for a marketplace token (RFC 8693), returning it as the account's `accessToken`. The subject token is sent only to a same-origin HTTPS token endpoint with redirects disabled. A marketplace that publishes no protected resource needs no bearer. The provider re-validates on `onDidChangeSessions('github'|'github-enterprise')`. Includes unit tests.
## How it maps to #325412

- ✅ GitHub auth-ENABLED path: RFC 8693 token exchange (raw GitHub token never reaches the resource server), client-side `checkAccess()` retained, no `/eligibility` POST.
- ✅ `onDidChangeSessions('github')` invalidation for the auth-enabled path.
- ✅ GitHub test-matrix scenarios (index `401` / no session / session + `checkAccess`, plus exchange failure and 403).

## Testing

- Unit tests in `extensionGalleryManifestService.test.ts` — the six GitHub scenarios above (55 gallery tests passing total).
- `typecheck-client` ✅ and `valid-layers-check` ✅.

## Open questions for review

- **`client_id` on the exchange.** The exchange currently sends **no `client_id`**. The server contract under-specifies the client side of the token endpoint, and OpenIddict token endpoints often require a `client_id`. This needs validation against a live GitHub-auth-enabled deployment; if required, a product-config override for the exchange `client_id` would be a small follow-up. This is the main reason the PR is opened as a **draft**.
- **Token refresh cadence.** The negotiated marketplace token is refreshed lazily (on the next not-Available re-validation), not on every routine GitHub session refresh, to avoid manifest flashes. The marketplace `at+jwt` has its own independent lifetime, so this is safe.

## Notes

- For an **open** (auth-disabled) GitHub marketplace deployment, the index is served anonymously, `getAccessToken()` returns `undefined`, and all requests stay anonymous — no behavior change.
- The token is only ever attached to same-secure-origin targets; never leaked cross-origin or over cleartext.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The changed line, helper implementation, and manifest call ordering directly prove the additional sequential HTTP boundary before startup can progress. The exact server delay varies, but the extra one-or-two request cardinality for metadata-absent marketplaces is deterministic.
Findings.PerformanceResource: HTTP network requests to protected-resource metadata endpoints
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Each marketplace bootstrap or GitHub account/session revalidation performs one failed metadata GET for an origin-only service URL, or two sequential failed GETs for a path-bearing service URL, before the service-index GET; the negative result is not cached.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased marketplace startup/revalidation latency from extra network round trips on the critical path
Findings.PreviousBehavior: For an eligible GitHub account, account resolution was local and the configured marketplace service index was fetched immediately, so an open marketplace required only the index request.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Every eligible GitHub account resolution now awaits protected-resource discovery before the manifest is requested, even when the marketplace is auth-disabled and publishes no protected-resource metadata.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added line `const protectedResource = await discoverMarketplaceProtectedResource(this.requestService, serviceIndexUrl);` unconditionally inserts metadata discovery into the GitHub account path; before this PR the GitHub provider returned immediately after the local eligibility check.
Findings.Title: Defer protected-resource discovery until the index challenges
Findings.Impact: Opening VS Code against an open GitHub-configured private marketplace now delays extension marketplace availability by at least one additional request round trip (two when the configured service URL contains a path). A slow or poorly routed `/.well-known` endpoint can hold the bootstrap much longer because this probe is awaited before the actual index request; session-change revalidations repeat the same delay.
Findings.Evidence: `doGetAccount` awaits `getMarketplaceAccessToken`, whose first operation at line 254 is `discoverMarketplaceProtectedResource`. `fetchResourceMetadata` tries the path-appended well-known URL and then the root URL sequentially when the configured URL has a path. `WorkbenchExtensionGalleryManifestService.handleMarketplaceAccountAccess` awaits `galleryAccountService.getAccount` before calling `getExtensionGalleryManifestFromServiceUrl`, so these optional probes are on the manifest critical path. The added open-index test still enters this code path but only asserts that no token exchange occurs, not that metadata discovery is skipped.
Findings.Recommendation: Fetch the service index anonymously first and only perform protected-resource discovery/token exchange after a 401/403 challenge, then retry the index with the exchanged token. If the flow cannot be challenge-driven, cache and coalesce both positive and negative discovery results per configured service URL so open marketplaces do not pay repeated probes.

Scenarios.Scenario: Bootstrap or revalidate an auth-disabled private marketplace with an eligible GitHub default account
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Marketplace availability waits for default-account resolution, then the newly added protected-resource discovery, then the existing service-index GET. The discovery is therefore directly on startup/revalidation's critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: GET protected-resource metadata from the well-known endpoint(s)
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One GET for an origin-only URL, or two sequential GETs when the configured service URL contains a path and metadata is absent
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The GitHub provider performed only a local eligibility check and proceeded directly to the index; there were no metadata probes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: All probes complete before the service index can be requested, adding their full latency to marketplace availability

ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: This was the first and only network request for an open GitHub marketplace.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Returns the manifest required for marketplace availability

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish the resolved manifest/token to the shared process and optional remote server
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One shared-process call plus one remote-server call when connected, after each newly fetched manifest
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Initial and account-triggered manifest updates already used the same channel fan-out.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Calls are not awaited, so they are off the bootstrap critical path

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One configured service URL per window. A root-only URL causes one failed metadata probe; a URL with a path causes two sequential probes (path-appended then root). Each GitHub/default-account revalidation repeats the probes because there is no negative cache.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Discovery attempts and the service-index request are awaited serially. Concurrent account-change events can overlap resolutions because cancellation is checked by the manifest service but the discovery requests use CancellationToken.None; event burst prevalence is not established strongly enough for a separate finding.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The manifest promise coalesces ordinary callers after bootstrap, but protected-resource discovery has neither positive/negative caching nor in-flight coalescing. Open-marketplace misses are repeated on account/session revalidation.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed await, metadata helper's sequential fallback, and manifest call ordering directly establish the mechanism.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Server RTT and behavior for unknown `/.well-known` routes vary, but the extra one-or-two serial requests and their critical-path placement are deterministic.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable startup/network latency regression: optional auth discovery is eagerly performed for open marketplaces before the index can load.

Scenarios.Scenario: Bootstrap and periodically refresh an RFC 8693-gated GitHub marketplace
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Cold bootstrap serially resolves protected-resource metadata, resolves authorization-server metadata, reads the matching GitHub session, exchanges the token, and fetches the service index. On the timer, the same path must finish before the refreshed manifest/token is published; channel publication itself is off-path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Normally one successful GET per cold bootstrap or token refresh; up to two sequential attempts for path-bearing URLs
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: GitHub account resolution performed no protected-resource discovery.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must complete before token exchange can proceed

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One successful GET in the normal case, up to three sequential discovery GETs on invalid or mismatched metadata
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No GitHub token-exchange metadata discovery existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must complete before the token endpoint is known

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One POST per successful discovery cycle, with redirects disabled
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No GitHub marketplace token exchange existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The returned bearer is required before fetching a gated index

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: GET protected marketplace service index with exchanged bearer
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One GET per resolution after exchange
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The index was fetched without a GitHub bearer and a gated deployment could not become available.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Returns the manifest required for progress

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish refreshed manifest/token to shared process and optional remote server
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One or two asynchronous channel calls per successful refresh
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: There was no periodic GitHub marketplace-token refresh to trigger this existing publication path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Not awaited; off the token-refresh critical path

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One configured marketplace per window. A successful cold/refresh cycle normally performs one PRM GET, one AS metadata GET when the first discovery URL succeeds, one token POST, and one index GET; malformed/mismatched AS metadata can expand discovery to three sequential GETs.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Operations within one resolution are serial. The refresh timer owns one disposable timeout and replaces the previous timer. Separate session/default-account events can start overlapping uncancelled network requests, but realistic aggregate burst size was not proven.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The exchanged access token remains published until an account event or refresh timer. Its expiry schedules refresh at 75% with bounds. PRM and AS metadata are not cached, so cold and refresh behavior have the same metadata call count; this periodic overhead is modest and tied to token lifetime, so it was not reported separately.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for call counts and serial ordering; medium for any user-visible impact beyond the reported open-marketplace case.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Token lifetimes and server RTTs vary. The serial call path is certain; the periodic metadata overhead is bounded to one marketplace and ordinarily once per 75% of token lifetime.
Scenarios.Verdict: The added boundaries are necessary for the gated feature and refresh is bounded by one timer. Static metadata caching could reduce periodic overhead, but the demonstrated scale does not justify another finding.

Scenarios.Scenario: Follow HTTP redirects through the Node request service
Scenarios.CriticalPath: A response with a 3xx and Location is resolved and then followed serially, as before. The diff adds URL parsing and a small header copy only for cross-origin redirects before issuing the same bounded follow-up request.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One follow-up request per accepted redirect, bounded by followRedirects (default three), unchanged from before
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The service already issued one recursive request per redirect; the diff changes URL resolution and credential forwarding, not request cardinality.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Each redirect remains on the originating request's critical path

Scenarios.ScalingInput: At most the configured redirect limit, default three. Header-copy CPU scales with the small request-header count only on cross-origin hops.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Redirects remain serial recursive requests; retries remain bounded to three idempotent attempts. The diff does not increase concurrency.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache participates in redirect handling.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the before/after diff preserves redirect count and recursion while adding only bounded local work.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Redirect prevalence varies, but changed CPU/allocation work is constant and tiny relative to the unchanged network hop.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable performance regression; boundary cardinality and critical-path network work are unchanged.

Scenarios.Scenario: Microsoft marketplace protected-resource discovery after helper extraction
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Eligible Microsoft account resolution still discovers protected-resource metadata before obtaining/using its resource token and fetching the index.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Same one-or-two sequential discovery attempts as before
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The removed Microsoft private helper performed the same request-service-backed `fetchResourceMetadata` operation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Remains on Microsoft account resolution's critical path

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One configured marketplace URL per account resolution, with the same one-or-two metadata discovery attempts as before.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Requests remain serial in the existing account-resolution path.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Existing Microsoft discovery/cache behavior is unchanged by moving the helper; the added `resource` field does not trigger additional work in the Microsoft path.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High from comparing the removed helper with the shared replacement.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: None material for PR causality; behavior is a refactor.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance regression; this is shared-helper extraction with unchanged network behavior.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all six changed files and traced startup, account/session revalidation, token refresh, redirect handling, metadata validation, and manifest publication. Submitted one finding for eager protected-resource discovery blocking open GitHub marketplace bootstrap; no concrete shipped regression fix requiring blame was identified.
